Work backwards from the magnetic moment to the number of unpaired electrons.
μ = √(n(n + 2))
1.75 = √(n(n + 2)) ⇒ n(n + 2) = 3.06
Try n = 1: 1 × 3 = 3, so μ = √3 = 1.73 BM ✓ — that is the match.
Now find the ion with exactly one unpaired electron. Remove the 4s electrons first:
Ti³⁺ : Ti is [Ar]3d²4s² ⇒ 3d¹ ⇒ n = 1, μ = 1.73 BM ✓
V³⁺ : [Ar]3d³4s² ⇒ 3d² ⇒ n = 2, μ = 2.83
Cr³⁺ : [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ ⇒ 3d³ ⇒ n = 3, μ = 3.87
Fe³⁺ : [Ar]3d⁶4s² ⇒ 3d⁵ ⇒ n = 5, μ = 5.92
Only titanium(III) gives 1.73 BM, which rounds to the 1.75 quoted.
∴ Ti³⁺.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|51||0|0.s:
Ionisation energy rises across a period, but nitrogen and oxygen break the trend.
The configurations are the reason:
N : 1s² 2s² 2p³ — a **half-filled** 2p subshell, which is extra stable, so removing an electron
is unusually hard.
O : 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ — the fourth p electron has to pair up in an orbital that already holds one.
That pairing brings electron–electron repulsion, so it comes out unusually easily.
The result is that oxygen's ionisation energy is **lower** than nitrogen's, reversing the
expected order.
Actual values in kJ mol⁻¹:
C 1086 < O 1314 < N 1402 < F 1681
So the increasing order is C < O < N < F.
The same anomaly appears one period down, between P and S.
∴ C < O < N < F.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|53||0|0.s:
Froth flotation is used for **sulphide** ores. It works because a sulphide surface is already
somewhat non-polar and is easily made water repellent by a collector such as potassium ethyl
xanthate, so the ore particles cling to air bubbles and rise with the froth while the silicate
gangue stays wetted and sinks.
Check the four ores:
(1) Chalcopyrites, CuFeS₂ — a sulphide ✓ concentrated by froth flotation
(3) Cuprite, Cu₂O — an oxide ✗
(4) Calamine, ZnCO₃ — a carbonate ✗
(2) Cryolite, Na₃AlF₆ — a fluoride, and not an ore being concentrated at all; it is the solvent
added during the electrolysis of alumina ✗
Oxide and carbonate ores are wetted by water and are concentrated by gravity separation or
magnetic separation instead.
∴ chalcopyrites.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|54||0|0.s:
Equivalent mass and atomic mass are linked by the valency:
equivalent mass = atomic mass / valency
The metal is bivalent, so valency = 2:
atomic mass = equivalent mass × valency = 20 × 2 = 40
A bivalent metal forms the chloride MCl₂, so its molecular mass is
M + 2 × 35.5 = 40 + 71 = 111
(The metal with atomic mass 40 and valency 2 is calcium, and CaCl₂ indeed has a formula mass
of 111.)
The word 'anhydrous' is there to warn against adding water of crystallisation — CaCl₂·2H₂O
would be 147.
Option (4), 75.5, comes from treating the metal as monovalent and adding only one chlorine.
∴ 111.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|55||0|0.s:
Two things change at once — the number of moles and the temperature — and the container is
closed, so the volume is fixed.
First the moles. N₂O₄ ⇒ 2NO₂, and 20% of the 2 mol decomposes:
N₂O₄ decomposed = 0.20 × 2 = 0.4 mol
NO₂ formed = 2 × 0.4 = 0.8 mol
N₂O₄ remaining = 2 − 0.4 = 1.6 mol
total moles = 1.6 + 0.8 = 2.4 mol
Now apply pV = nRT at constant V:
p₂/p₁ = (n₂T₂)/(n₁T₁)
p₂/1 = (2.4 × 596)/(2 × 298)
The temperature has exactly doubled, so 596/298 = 2:
p₂ = (2.4/2) × 2 = 2.4 atm
Both effects matter — the mole increase alone would give 1.2 atm, the heating alone 2 atm.
∴ 2.4 atm.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|56||0|0.s:
A reducing sugar is one that can open its ring to expose a free aldehyde group, or a keto
group next to a CHOH that can tautomerise to one. That free carbonyl is what reduces
Tollens' and Fehling's reagents.
In glucose and fructose one anomeric carbon is left free, so the ring can open and they are
reducing. The same is true of maltose and lactose.
Sucrose is different. It is glucose joined to fructose through **both** of their anomeric
carbons — C-1 of glucose to C-2 of fructose. With both tied up in the glycosidic link, neither
ring can open, so no free aldehyde or keto group can ever appear.
Hence it gives no reaction with Fehling's or Tollens' reagent.
(1) and (4) are true statements about sucrose but have nothing to do with reducing power,
and (3) is true of the reducing sugar fructose as well, so it cannot be the reason.
∴ because it contains no free aldehyde or keto group adjacent to a CHOH group.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|58||0|0.s:
Dialysis separates a **colloid** from a **crystalloid** using a parchment or cellophane membrane.
The pores let small, true-solution particles pass through, but colloidal particles (1–1000 nm)
are too large and are held back.
So the method only works when one component is colloidal and the other is not.
(3) Glucose is a crystalloid and passes through the membrane; protein is a macromolecular
colloid and stays behind ✓ The two separate cleanly.
(1) Glucose and fructose are both crystalloids — both pass through, no separation.
(4) Glucose and NaCl are both crystalloids — same problem.
(2) Protein and starch are both colloids — both are retained, so neither passes.
This is how a dialysis machine cleans blood: urea and salts diffuse out while the blood
proteins and cells are kept.
∴ glucose and protein.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|59||0|0.s:
The percentage of p-character is the share of p orbitals among the orbitals mixed.
Graphite — each carbon is bonded to three others in flat sheets, so it is **sp²**. That mixes
one s orbital with two p orbitals, three in total:
p-character = 2/3 = 66.7% ≈ 67%
Diamond — each carbon is bonded to four others tetrahedrally, so it is **sp³**. One s with
three p, four in total:
p-character = 3/4 = 75%
So graphite 67%, diamond 75%, in that order.
The s-character is the complement, 33% and 25%, which is option (1) — the same numbers with
the question read backwards.
It is worth remembering that greater s-character means a shorter, stronger bond, which is why
the C–C bond in graphite (142 pm) is shorter than in diamond (154 pm).
∴ 67 and 75.

kcet|Chemistry|2012|60||0|0.s:
This is work done against a **constant** external pressure, so
w = p(external) × ΔV
ΔV = V₂ − V₁ = 2 − 1 = 1 m³
p = 10⁵ N m⁻²
w = 10⁵ × 1 = 10⁵ N m = 10⁵ J
Convert to kilojoules:
10⁵ J = 100 kJ = 10² kJ
Check the units: N m⁻² × m³ = N m = J ✓ — no conversion factor is needed because the data
are already in SI.
The gas is **expanding**, so it does work on the surroundings; by the sign convention the work
done *by* the gas is positive, and the internal energy falls by this amount if no heat enters.
Options (3) and (4) quote joules but with the wrong exponent.
∴ 10² kJ.
